# 4.2 – Understanding Slope {.unnumbered}

In the previous lesson, you learned how to create tables of values for a linear function to create a graph. 
Different linear functions produced different graphs but they all produced straight lines. 

In real-world situations, it is often useful to compare functions by looking at their graphs.

In this lesson, you will learn how to describe the way that lines change as you move from left to right.
This rate of change is called the **slope**, one of the most important concepts you will learn in algebra.

:::{.objectives}

- [ ] I can find the slope of a line from a graph or from two points.
- [ ] I can describe slope as a rate of change between x and y.
- [ ] I can tell whether a slope is positive, negative, zero, or undefined.
- [ ] I can explain why vertical lines do not have a slope.

:::

:::{.vocab}

{{< glink slope >}}, {{< glink rise >}}, {{< glink run >}}, {{< glink rate of change >}}, {{< glink horizontal line >}}, {{< glink vertical line >}}

:::

{{< warmup >}}

1. Plot the function $f(x) = 2x + 1$.

2. On the same graph, plot the function $g(x) = -3x + 1$.

3. Looking at your graph. How are the two lines the same? How are they different?
   [plot of two lines with same intercept but different slopes]


{{< learn >}}

### 4.2.1 – What Is Slope?

Look at the image below. In each of the four panels, a person is climbing stairs. How are the four images similar? How are they different?

![](/images/Unit_4/Lesson_2/stairs_xkcd.png){width=350px fig-align="center"}

You probably notice that the stairs in panels A and D are far less steep than the stairs in panels B and C. You may also notice that the stairs in panels A and C move up and to the right while the ones in panels B and D move down.

Linear functions are the same. Sometimes they go up as we move to the right, and sometimes they go down. Sometimes they are steep, and other times they are less so. Together, direction and steepness describe the **slope**.

The slope tells how much we rise (up or down) for every step we move to the right — it’s a rate of change. A larger slope means the line rises or falls more sharply — the {{< glink vertical >}} change happens faster for each {{< glink horizontal >}} step to the right.

On a graph, the **rise** is a change in $y$ (abbreviated as $\Delta y$) and the **run** is a change in $x$ (abbreviated as $\Delta x$). 

The slope, often abbreviated as $m$, is simply:

$$
m = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}
$$

:::{.think title="How does the rise (change in y) compare to the run (change in x) in each of the 4 panels above?"}

|   Panel  |   Direction | Rise Compared to Run | $m=\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$ |
|   :-:    |   :-:    | :-: |  :-:  |
|   A      |   Positive (up) | About half as fast | $\frac{1}{2}$ |
|   B      |   Negative (down) | About the same   | $\frac{-1}{1}$ |
|   C      |   Positive     |   About the same | $\frac{1}{1}$ |
|   D      |   Negative     |  About half as fast |  $\frac{-1}{2}$ |

:::


---

### 4.2.2 – Finding Slope From a Graph

* To find slope from a graph, pick two clear points on the line.
* Count the **rise** (change in y) and the **run** (change in x).
* Then use (m = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}).

![](/images/Unit_4/Lesson_2/rise_run_example.png){width="300px" fig-align="center"}

:::{.think title="Reading Direction"}
Always read slope **left to right**, like you read a sentence.
:::

:::{.you-try title="Count the slope"}
Find the rise and run between two points on your graph, then compute (m = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}).
:::

---

### 4.2.3 – Types of Slope

| Type          | Description               | Example  |
| ------------- | ------------------------- | -------- |
| **Positive**  | Line rises left to right  | (m > 0)  |
| **Negative**  | Line falls left to right  | (m < 0)  |
| **Zero**      | Line is flat (horizontal) | (y = 3)  |
| **Undefined** | Line is vertical (no run) | (x = -2) |

:::{.real-world title="What They Mean"}

* **Positive slope:** going uphill, savings increasing, temperature rising.
* **Negative slope:** going downhill, spending money, cooling down.
* **Zero slope:** no change — a flat road or steady balance.
* **Undefined slope:** vertical line — you’d have to “divide by zero,” which doesn’t make sense.
:::

:::{.you-try-m title="Sketch examples"}
Draw one example of each type of slope on graph paper. Label each line with its slope.
:::

:::{.think title="When Two Lines Meet"}
If two lines have different slopes, they’ll **cross at one point**.  
That point has the same (x, y) values in both equations — it makes **both** true.
:::

---

### 4.2.4 – Slope in the Real World

:::{.real-world title="Comparing Slopes in Context"}

* A **wheelchair ramp** that rises 1 foot for every 12 feet forward has a slope of ( \frac{1}{12} ).
* A **hill** that rises 10 feet for every 20 feet forward has a slope of ( \frac{10}{20} = \frac{1}{2} ).
  Which one is steeper?
:::

:::{.real-world title="Rates as Slopes"}

* A car traveling 60 miles per hour and a cyclist traveling 15 miles per hour both form straight lines on a distance-time graph.
* The car’s line is steeper because its **slope (rate of change)** is greater.
:::

:::{.think title="What Slope Tells Us"}
The larger the slope, the faster the change.
The smaller the slope, the slower or flatter the change.
:::

---

:::{.remember title="Key Idea"}
Slope measures how y changes compared to x.
A **constant slope** means the line rises or falls evenly — that’s what makes it *linear*.
:::
